title: DESNZ on Clean Power, grid bottlenecks, bills and resilience
label: 14 October 2026 · DESNZ scrutiny
summary: The Secretary of State and Permanent Secretary outlined progress towards the Clean Power 2030 target, acknowledged serious grid and delivery bottlenecks, and emphasised affordability, system reform and security. They defended existing tools like Contracts for Difference, set out the aim of a new Great British Grid public operator to accelerate network build‑out, committed to supporting home‑upgrade and heat technology rollout, and said nuclear and storage decisions are being progressed while they review regulation and resilience, including cyber and physical threats.

glossary.definition: A UK government target to increase government-backed low‑carbon electricity capacity by 2030.
Contracts for Difference: a government scheme that guarantees a set price to low‑carbon generators to encourage investment.
The UK energy regulator responsible for enforcing market rules and setting network incentives.
National Electricity System Operator, responsible for running and planning the electricity system in Great Britain.
A regulatory mechanism that limits revenue risks for major energy infrastructure projects by setting upper and lower revenue bands.
Carbon capture, utilisation and storage: technology to capture CO2 from industry or power generation and store it underground.
A government programme to upgrade households' energy efficiency and lift people out of fuel poverty.
A grants programme to encourage households to replace fossil-fuel heating with low‑carbon alternatives.
A government framework to streamline approvals and support for new nuclear technologies.
A proposed public-sector body to speed up electricity transmission planning and build‑out.
The independent regulator that enforces nuclear safety and security in Great Britain.

chapters.title: Progress on Clean Power 2030
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say the UK has unlocked large clean power investment and made progress but delivery faces network and planning bottlenecks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How well are we doing on the Clean Power 2030 target?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: The target has built momentum. We've unlocked around £100bn of investment, consented capacity for over 20 million homes, and renewables supplied the system two-thirds of the time last year. Progress is real, but more work is needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Developers tell us projects are blocked by grid gates: solar‑plus‑storage get stuck because they sit in different queue stages. Does the system need an overhaul?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: Parts of the system share the same ambition but struggle because of historic underinvestment in networks. We reordered queues, launched Great British Grid to accelerate build‑out, and are working with operators on workforce and practical barriers.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: Ofgem, NESO and DESNZ want the same outcome. The issue is scale and complexity: planning resource, grid queue ordering and execution need to speed up. We're stabilising connections but it's a big job.

chapters.title: Regulator independence vs policy delivery
chapters.takeaway: Government recognises tensions between regulator independence and delivering strategic policy, especially for cost‑effective long‑duration storage.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Some allege Ofgem favours up‑front cost over lifetime value, excluding longer‑term solutions. Does that conflict with ministers' policy?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: We hear those frustrations and want change. We back innovation and schemes that support long‑duration storage; where companies challenge outcomes, Ofgem has consulted and will respond.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: Regulator independence means Ofgem implements policy. Government is firming up policy statements so the regulator and industry know what to deliver; some high‑CAPEX, long‑benefit projects have already passed mind‑to decisions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are you committed to using CfDs for solar?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: CfDs have been effective in unlocking investment. We'll keep using them where they make sense while balancing incentives against consumer costs.

chapters.title: Affordability and decoupling from gas
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say home‑grown clean power is essential to reduce exposure to volatile global gas prices, but system reform and network build‑out are also needed.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: With UK prices among the highest in Europe, what is the plan to bring energy costs down?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: Affordability is the top priority. Short‑term relief includes VAT removal and targeted support, but long‑term we must deploy home‑grown clean energy, reform market structure, and invest in critical infrastructure and fair cost allocation.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: If grid build‑out lags, can we decouple electricity prices from international gas?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: Decoupling is under way: more renewables on the system reduces gas influence and CfDs fix renewable prices. But network constraints remain and must be tackled so renewables can connect and displace gas.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: Is Government funding for networks sufficient?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: We are funding key parts and using recovery mechanisms, but industry flags workforce and practical constraints more than lack of funding. We will work in step with industry to resolve those barriers.

chapters.title: Warm Homes, heat technologies and local delivery
chapters.takeaway: Government will keep funding warm homes programmes and widen technology support, but delivery needs local capability and clearer standards.

turns.speaker: Wera Hobhouse
turns.text: You are adding heat batteries. Why are other proven options like electric boilers excluded from grants and standards?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: We judge technologies by ease of adoption, emissions impact and need for subsidy. The Boiler Upgrade Scheme has broadened over time; we're open to reviewing other technologies and will look into the company you mentioned.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We work closely with BSI on standards. Criteria exist to ensure public money is used properly, but we're ready to adjust as technology changes and invite innovators to engage with the innovation team.

turns.speaker: Lizzi Collinge
turns.text: Warm Homes grants show postcode variation and local authorities with no delivery capacity struggle because grants are paid in arrears. Will devolution help?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: Devolution should help by enabling area‑based upgrades and blending funds. We'll establish a Warm Homes agency in shadow form to support places lacking capacity and evolve the scheme with local feedback.

turns.speaker: Lizzi Collinge
turns.text: Will the zero VAT on solar materials be extended?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: We have asked the Chancellor but tax matters are his decision.

chapters.title: Nuclear regulation, sites and the Fingleton agenda
chapters.takeaway: The Department is implementing Fingleton recommendations, pushing legislation where needed, and seeking clearer regulatory rules to balance safety with strategic energy needs.

turns.speaker: Lizzi Collinge
turns.text: Old planning criteria prevent some new nuclear sites. When will those criteria and Fingleton recommendations be implemented?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We're working through all 47 Fingleton recommendations. Some need legislation; others don't. We will provide a written update on progress and timings.

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: We want a swift Bill but need parliamentary time. We recognise industry urgency and are pressing for a slot; some reform can be done without legislation and is already happening.

turns.speaker: Lizzi Collinge
turns.text: Should the Office for Nuclear Regulation be required to weigh strategic objectives—like energy security—into safety decisions?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: Policy intent is that strategic factors are considered. We will look at the most appropriate mechanism to ensure they feed into regulatory decision‑making.

turns.speaker: Claire Young
turns.text: What role will GB Energy‑North and GBE‑N sites play, and is their engagement with local authorities clear?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: GBE‑N are identifying potential sites; we will follow up on transparency and engagement concerns. ANF work and site allocation are being coordinated with industry.

chapters.title: Security, resilience and accountability
chapters.takeaway: Ministers said the UK has robust contingency arrangements for physical and cyber threats, will continue testing, and that DESNZ must lead strategic coordination across bodies.

turns.speaker: Torcuil Crichton
turns.text: Can you assure consumers the lights won't go out this winter?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: I'm 100% confident we will not have national outages this winter. We have tested the system and have diverse supply and contingency plans.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: With recent attacks on energy infrastructure abroad, who decides and acts if something happens to offshore assets here?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: We have a cross‑government framework including the security services; serious incidents would go to COBRA. If companies feel unclear who to call, they should come to us.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: Are cyber and AI‑driven threats being factored into plans?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: Yes. We work with NCSC, Ofgem and others; new legislation will broaden powers and supply‑chain oversight. Resilience work is ongoing and must evolve with the threat.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who is ultimately accountable for fixing the coordination between DESNZ, Ofgem, NESO and others?

turns.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
turns.text: Ultimately me. We accept the system is noisy; DESNZ will set clearer strategic direction and strengthen coordination. GB Grid and other reforms aim to simplify delivery.
